paragraphs.heading: Two lines and the angle between
paragraphs.text: Axial tilt, also called obliquity, is the angle between the line a body spins around and the line standing at right angles to the flat plane of its orbit. For Earth, the spin axis is the imaginary line through the North and South Poles. The orbital axis is the line at right angles to the plane Earth moves in as it circles the Sun. A tilt of 0 degrees would mean both lines point the same way, so the spin axis stands straight up from the orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Why we have seasons
paragraphs.text: Over a single orbit the tilt barely changes, and the axis keeps pointing the same way against the stars. That habit is called axial parallelism. As a result, for part of the orbit one pole leans sunward, and half a year later that same pole leans away. This is what gives Earth its seasons: the Northern Hemisphere has summer when the North Pole leans sunward and the South Pole leans away.

paragraphs.heading: Earth's number today
paragraphs.text: Astronomers call the plane of Earth's orbit the ecliptic, and they call Earth's tilt the obliquity of the ecliptic, written with the Greek letter ε. Right now it is about 23.44°. It is not a fixed quantity, because tugs from the planets make the ecliptic itself move. At present the tilt is shrinking by about 46.8″ per century.

paragraphs.heading: A 41,000-year rhythm
paragraphs.text: Computer simulations of the Solar System over millions of years show how the tilt wanders. Across the past 5 million years it has moved back and forth between 22°2′33″ and 24°30′16″. The average length of one cycle is 41,040 years. This cycle blends precession with the largest term in the ecliptic's own motion. For the next million years it should swing between 22°13′44″ and 24°20′50″. Shifts in the tilt can affect the seasons, and they are likely one of the things behind climate change over long spans of time.

paragraphs.heading: The Moon as a steadier
paragraphs.text: The Moon helps keep Earth's tilt steady. A 1993 study suggested that without the Moon, resonances and chaotic behavior in the Solar System could drive the tilt as high as 90° within a few million years. Simulations in 2011 gave a calmer answer, with swings of only about 20 to 25°. Later work on how fast the tilt can drift found it would take more than billions of years to come near 90°. The Moon's steadying hand will last less than two billion years, and as the Moon keeps drifting away, resonances may bring large swings in the tilt.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring it through history
paragraphs.text: People have measured the tilt for a very long time. Around 350 BCE, Pytheas of Marseilles took a measurement at the summer solstice from the shadow cast by a gnomon. About 830 CE, the Caliph Al-Mamun of Baghdad had his astronomers measure it, and their result served the Arab world for many years. In 1437 Ulugh Beg found a value of 23°30′17″. In 1538 Fracastoro was the first to see that the tilt is shrinking at a fairly steady rate.
